# Components of positioning

## Directives

From [Digital product development](digital-product-development.md):

- Name the user and the task of each feature before you design or build the feature. ^name-user-and-task

From [Product strategy](product-strategy.md):

- State the user problem of each feature in one sentence. ^state-user-problem
- Write the success measure of each feature before you build the feature. ^write-success-measure

From [Product positioning](product-positioning.md):

- Do not start positioning work from a fill-in positioning statement. ^no-fill-in-statement
- Write the positioning of a product before you write its messaging. ^positioning-before-messaging

From [Components of positioning](positioning-components.md):

- Choose an existing market category for the product, unless the company decides to create a new category. ^choose-existing-category
- If the company creates a new market category, explain the category to customers as the first step of its positioning. ^define-new-category
- If the product beats the category leaders only for one kind of buyer, add that niche to the category name. ^name-category-niche
- Do not list a competitor that customers do not compare with the product. ^no-phantom-competitors
- Define the components of positioning in this order: alternatives, unique attributes, value, target customers, and market category. ^positioning-order
- List the alternatives that customers use today, including doing nothing or a manual process. ^real-alternatives
- Describe the target customers by the traits that make them care most about the value. ^target-by-traits
- Link each value claim to a unique attribute that the alternatives lack. ^value-from-attributes

## Definition

The five parts of positioning in April Dunford's method. Competitive alternatives are what customers would do if the product did not exist, including nothing at all. Unique attributes are the capabilities that the product has and the alternatives lack. Value is the benefit that those attributes give to customers. Target customers are the customers who care a lot about that value. The market category is the context that makes the value obvious to those customers. Each component depends on the others, so the method starts with the alternatives and works through the list in order.

## Notes

Dunford took the starting point from Jobs to Be Done: what customers would do without the product decides what counts as unique. A spreadsheet, a manual process, or an intern can be the real alternative. In enterprise software, Dunford reports that about a quarter of deals end in no decision, so the status quo is a competitor.

A phantom competitor is a company that could compete in theory but never shows up in deals. Positioning against it weakens the positioning. A new market category must first gain a meaning in the minds of customers before it gives any context, and the companies that create a category often lose it to later entrants.
